name: SpiderFoot
purpose: OSINT automation platform with 200-plus modules that take a seed (domain, IP, email, name) and query many data sources automatically, correlating results into an entity graph with a web interface.
journalism_use_case: Automated first-pass reconnaissance on an entity: give it a company domain and it queries dozens of sources — DNS, certificates, breach data, social platforms, scan databases — assembling a correlated picture that would take a day by hand.
pros: Module breadth means a single scan covers ground that would otherwise require a dozen tools, which is genuinely time-saving on a new target
Correlation into an entity graph surfaces relationships between findings rather than leaving you with a dozen separate outputs
Web interface makes it usable by an investigator who is not comfortable in a terminal, which widens who can run reconnaissance
Open source and self-hosted, so scan results stay with you
cons: Automated breadth is also the problem: a full scan queries many third-party services, disclosing your target to all of them, and some modules actively probe — so the operational-security footprint of one click is large and poorly visible
Output volume is substantial and noisy; the correlation helps but separating signal from parked domains, breach-data false positives and stale records takes real work
Many modules need API keys, several paid, so an unconfigured SpiderFoot delivers much less than its module count suggests
Commercial version (SpiderFoot HX) exists, so the open edition's feature boundary and development priority warrant checking
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived. SpiderFoot is well known in the OSINT community and the commercial HX edition is documented by the vendor.
assessment: Pilot it with modules deliberately selected rather than running everything — the default breadth makes a single scan a broad disclosure of your target to dozens of third parties, which for a surveillance-industry investigation is the wrong trade. For your profile the better pattern is usually a small set of chosen tools (subfinder, httpx, asn, certstream) whose disclosure you understand, with SpiderFoot reserved for low-sensitivity targets where speed matters more than discretion.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived, with activity patterns consistent with an open edition maintained alongside a commercial product. Classified stable-low; verify the open edition's current development before depending on it.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file; open edition alongside a commercial product)
model_or_data_licence: Third-party data sources have their own terms; several restrict redistribution of results.
licence_restrictions: Permissive as published. Data-source terms are the practical constraint, particularly for breach-data modules whose use and republication raise separate legal and ethical questions.
costs: No fee for the open edition. Many modules require paid API keys (not priced here), so realistic capability has a recurring cost. SpiderFoot HX is a separate commercial product. Estimate.
privacy: The weakest point: a broad scan discloses your target to dozens of third-party services simultaneously, and active modules touch the target directly. Select modules deliberately and use a dedicated egress.
alternatives: A curated chain (subfinder, httpx, asn, certstream) whose disclosure footprint you understand
Maltego for graph-based OSINT with commercial transforms
recon-ng for a modular framework with explicit per-module execution
blockers: A full scan discloses the target to many third parties at once and includes active probing

name: recon-ng
purpose: Modular reconnaissance framework with a Metasploit-style interactive console, independent modules for discovery and enrichment, and a workspace database for accumulating results.
journalism_use_case: Reconnaissance where you choose each step: run a specific module against a target, see what it returns, then decide the next module — which keeps the disclosure footprint under control, unlike an automated scan that queries everything at once.
pros: Explicit per-module execution is the operational-security advantage over SpiderFoot: you know exactly which third party you just told about your target, because you chose it
Workspace database accumulates findings across sessions, so a long investigation's reconnaissance builds rather than restarting
Modular architecture makes writing a module for a source specific to your region a contained task
Long-established with a familiar console idiom for anyone with security-tooling background
cons: Maintenance has slowed considerably, and several modules depend on sources whose access has degraded or disappeared — so module breakage is common and often silent
Console idiom is unfamiliar to journalists and the learning curve is steeper than a CLI tool with flags
Many modules require API keys, some paid
Security-tooling framing throughout, so adapting the mental model to journalism takes effort
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with reduced activity. The broader degradation of search-engine and free-API sources documented elsewhere in this catalogue (pagodo, dorks_hunter, theHarvester) affects recon-ng's modules equally.
assessment: Monitor rather than adopt: the deliberate per-module approach is the right instinct, but the framework's slowed maintenance against degraded sources means many modules no longer work. For your profile the same discipline is better achieved with a small set of individually maintained tools you invoke explicitly — subfinder, httpx, asn — where you can see each tool's health rather than discovering a module has silently returned nothing.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived, but with substantially reduced activity relative to the project's earlier period and a module ecosystem dependent on sources that have degraded. Declining rather than dormant; no deprecation notice.
licence: GPL-3.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Third-party sources have their own terms.
licence_restrictions: Copyleft on the framework; immaterial for internal use.
costs: No fee. API keys for several modules, some paid (not priced here). Negligible compute.
privacy: Better than an automated scanner because you choose each module and therefore each disclosure. Individual modules may actively probe — check before running.
alternatives: A curated set of individually maintained CLI tools, which is what I would actually use
SpiderFoot for automated breadth, accepting the disclosure
Maltego for a graph-oriented commercial alternative
blockers: Slowed maintenance against degraded data sources means silent module failure

name: NetworkX
purpose: Python library for creating, manipulating and analysing graphs and networks, with a comprehensive collection of algorithms for centrality, community detection, paths, flows and structural analysis.
journalism_use_case: The analytical layer for any relationship question: compute who sits at the centre of a corporate network, find the shortest ownership path between two entities, detect communities in a co-sharing network, or identify the broker whose removal disconnects a cluster — the findings that turn a graph picture into a reportable claim.
pros: Algorithm breadth is the point: centrality, community detection and path analysis are what produce findings, and NetworkX implements essentially all of them with documented definitions you can cite
Pure Python with a clear API, so a data journalist can compute a betweenness centrality without learning a graph database
BSD-3-Clause under NumFOCUS governance with exceptional maintenance (release 3.6.1 2026-02-13 era line, pushed 2026-11-17) — stable, long-lived and institutionally supported
Integrates with the whole Python data stack and exports to Gephi for visualisation, so analysis and presentation connect cleanly
cons: Pure Python means performance limits: graphs beyond a few hundred thousand edges become slow, where igraph or a graph database is appropriate

Centrality metrics are easy to compute and easy to over-interpret — 'most central' is a mathematical property of your graph construction, not a finding about real-world importance, and that distinction is routinely lost in published network journalism
Graph construction decisions (what counts as an edge, which entities are included) determine the results entirely, and the library cannot help you make them defensibly
No visualisation worth publishing; Gephi or a web library is needed for the graphic
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived under NumFOCUS-affiliated governance with same-day commits. NetworkX is the standard Python graph library, well established across scientific computing and data journalism.
assessment: Adopt it as the standard link-analysis tool — the algorithms are what produce findings and the documentation lets you cite definitions precisely. For your profile the methodological discipline matters more than the code: state how edges were defined, publish the construction rules, and never present a centrality score as a claim about real-world power without corroboration. Move to igraph when performance binds.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with same-day commits, under NumFOCUS-affiliated community governance and a long, consistent release history. Among the most dependable maintenance profiles in this catalogue.
costs: No fee. CPU and memory proportional to graph size; pure-Python performance is the limiting factor rather than cost. Estimate.
alternatives: igraph for substantially better performance on large graphs
Gephi for interactive visualisation and layout
Neo4j where the graph is persistent and queried by several people

name: igraph
purpose: C library for graph analysis with bindings for Python, R and Mathematica, implementing a wide range of algorithms with performance suitable for large graphs.
journalism_use_case: The same link analysis as NetworkX at a scale NetworkX cannot reach: community detection and centrality over a co-sharing network of millions of edges, or a corporate graph assembled from a national register, where pure-Python performance would make the analysis impractical.
pros: C implementation gives order-of-magnitude performance over NetworkX on large graphs, which is what makes million-edge analysis feasible on a workstation
R bindings matter for this field: much coordinated-behaviour and network research is in R, so igraph lets you use published methods directly (CooRTweet depends on it)
Comprehensive algorithm coverage comparable to NetworkX, so switching for performance does not mean losing capability
Long-established with GPL-2.0 licensing and stable maintenance
cons: GPL-2.0 copyleft is a consideration if you embed it in a distributed product, though not for internal analysis
C library plus bindings means installation is less trivial than a pure-Python package, particularly on Windows
Same interpretive hazard as NetworkX: performance makes it easier to compute metrics over large graphs and no easier to interpret them responsibly
API differs from NetworkX, so porting an analysis between them is real work rather than a rename
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with continuing development. igraph's use in network science is well established, and CooRTweet's dependency on the R bindings is verifiable from that project.
assessment: Adopt it when graph size defeats NetworkX, and specifically when you want to use R-based published methods for coordinated-behaviour analysis — that is a concrete reason to have it. For your profile the pragmatic approach is NetworkX by default for its API clarity, igraph when a computation does not finish, and the same methodological discipline about edge definition and interpretation in both cases.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with continuing development across the C core and language bindings. A long-established project with consistent maintenance.
licence: GPL-2.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
licence_restrictions: GPL-2.0 copyleft: embedding in a distributed product triggers obligations. Internal analysis is unaffected.
costs: No fee. CPU and memory proportional to graph size, with much better constants than NetworkX. Estimate.
alternatives: NetworkX for clearer Python API at smaller scale
graph-tool for another high-performance option with different licensing
Neo4j or DuckDB where persistence and querying matter more than algorithm breadth

name: Gephi
purpose: Desktop application for interactive network visualisation and exploration, with force-directed layouts, filtering, community detection, statistics and publication-quality export.
journalism_use_case: Exploring and presenting a network: load a co-sharing graph or a corporate-ownership network, apply a layout, colour by community, filter to the dense core, and export a figure for publication — the step that turns an edge list into something a reader can understand.
pros: Interactive layout and filtering is how you actually understand a network — static analysis tells you metrics, but seeing the structure is what generates the reporting questions
No-code operation makes it usable by an analyst without Python, which widens who can do network work in a newsroom
Publication-quality export means the figure in the story comes from the same tool as the analysis, reducing the chance of a mismatch
Long-established standard in network visualisation with a consortium behind it, widely taught
cons: Force-directed layouts are seductive and misleading: visual proximity is an artefact of the layout algorithm and its random seed, not a measure of relationship strength, and readers (and journalists) consistently over-read it
Java desktop application with a history of version and platform friction, and performance degrades on large graphs — tens of thousands of nodes is comfortable, hundreds of thousands is not
Development pace is modest, with long gaps between releases historically
Easy to produce a beautiful graphic that supports a claim the data does not, which is the central risk in network journalism
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived under consortium governance with modest release cadence. Gephi's standing as the standard network-visualisation tool is well established in both research and journalism.
assessment: Adopt it for exploration and figure production, with an explicit rule about what the figure claims. For your profile the discipline that matters: a published network graphic must state how edges were defined, and the caption should not imply that visual clustering means organisational relationship unless you have evidence beyond the layout. Compute the metrics in NetworkX or igraph and use Gephi to see and show the structure — not to discover claims.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under Gephi Consortium governance, with a modest release cadence consistent with the project's long history. Classified stable-low: a mature application maintained rather than actively expanded.
licence: GPL-3.0 and CDDL dual licensing (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence files)
licence_restrictions: Copyleft on the application; immaterial for desktop analytical use. The dual-licence structure is worth reading if you distribute plugins.
costs: No fee. An analyst workstation with adequate RAM; large graphs need more. Java runtime. Estimate.
privacy: Entirely local; graph data stays on the machine. Some plugins fetch external data — check before use on a sensitive graph.
alternatives: sigma.js or Cytoscape.js for web-published interactive networks
Cytoscape for biological-network-oriented analysis with different algorithm emphasis
NetworkX plus matplotlib for scripted, reproducible figures

name: sigma.js
maintainer: Alexis Jacomy and the sigma.js community
purpose: JavaScript library for rendering interactive network graphs in the browser using WebGL, with layouts, camera controls and event handling, built on the graphology data structure.
journalism_use_case: Publishing an interactive network with a story: readers explore a corporate-ownership or co-sharing graph themselves, clicking entities to see details — which makes a complex network comprehensible in a way a static figure cannot.
pros: WebGL rendering handles graphs large enough to be interesting in the browser, where SVG-based libraries stall
Pairs with graphology for in-browser graph manipulation, so filtering and metric computation can happen client-side as the reader explores
MIT licensed with active maintenance and a focused scope, maintained by people embedded in the network-analysis community
Interactive exploration lets a reader verify a claim about the network themselves, which is a genuine transparency gain over a static image
cons: Engineering effort: a published interactive network is a front-end project, not a configuration, and the design work (what is clickable, what is shown, how to avoid misleading layout) is substantial
Same layout-misinterpretation risk as Gephi, amplified because readers will draw conclusions from positions you did not intend
Large graphs still need thinning before publication, so the dataset shown is a curated subset and that curation needs explaining
Bundle weight and GPU requirements affect readers on constrained devices — the same reach consideration as MapLibre versus Leaflet
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with active development. sigma.js is a recognised library in web network visualisation, used alongside graphology in the network-analysis ecosystem.
assessment: Integrate it where an interactive network genuinely helps the reader — which is less often than it is used, since many networks are better communicated as a curated figure plus a table. For your profile, if you do publish one, state the edge definition in the interface itself and consider annotating the specific relationships the story relies on, so a reader exploring the graph finds the claims rather than inventing their own from the layout.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with continuing development alongside the graphology data-structure library. Community-maintained with people active in the network-analysis field.
costs: No fee. Front-end development time is the real cost. Negligible hosting.
privacy: Client-side rendering; the graph data is published to readers by definition, so what you include is a disclosure decision.
alternatives: Gephi export to a static figure, which is simpler and often clearer
Cytoscape.js as an alternative web graph library with different strengths
A table plus a curated diagram, which for many networks communicates better than an interactive graph

name: Neo4j Community Edition
purpose: Graph database with the Cypher query language, ACID transactions, indexing and a browser interface, available as a GPL-3-licensed Community Edition and commercial Enterprise editions.
journalism_use_case: A persistent, queryable investigation graph that several people share: load entities and relationships from leaks, registries and sanctions data, then answer questions in Cypher — 'find paths of length three between this politician and this company' — interactively rather than by rerunning a script.
pros: Cypher makes relationship queries expressible and readable, which matters when an analyst rather than an engineer needs to ask the next question — path queries in particular are awkward in SQL and natural here
Persistent and multi-user, so an investigation graph becomes shared infrastructure rather than one person's notebook state
Browser interface lets a non-engineer explore and visualise query results directly, lowering the barrier to using the graph
Community Edition is GPL-3 licensed and free to download (verified on the vendor pricing page), so the capability is genuinely available without a licence purchase
cons: Community Edition is deliberately limited — single database, no clustering, no role-based access control — and the Enterprise features that a multi-user newsroom might want are quote-only with no public price (verified on the vendor pricing page 2026-11-16)
GPL-3 on the Community Edition constrains embedding it in a distributed product, and the licensing split is a deliberate commercial funnel
Operating a JVM graph database with adequate memory is real infrastructure, and a badly tuned Neo4j performs poorly in ways that look like a data problem
AuraDB, the managed option, is priced per GB-hour (from $0.09/GB/hour Professional, from $0.20/GB/hour Business Critical, verified 2026-11-16) and places your investigation graph in a vendor's cloud
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented pricing, verified on the vendor page 2026-11-16 and recorded in sources/recovered/cat/pricing.tsv: Community Edition GPL-3 and free to download; Enterprise and Infinigraph editions contact-sales (quote required); AuraDB Free $0, Professional from $0.09/GB/hour (minimum 1GB), Business Critical from $0.20/GB/hour (minimum 2GB), with hourly metering including storage, compute, IO, network and backups.
assessment: Adopt the Community Edition for a shared investigation graph where Cypher's expressiveness earns its operational cost — which is mainly when several people need to ask relationship questions over months. For your profile avoid AuraDB for investigation data: per-GB-hour billing on a graph you will keep for years is both expensive and a custody decision. If Community Edition's single-database and access-control limits bind, consider whether DuckDB or a FollowTheMoney-based store would serve, since Enterprise pricing is quote-only.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with continuous development under commercial maintenance. Vendor pricing page verified 2026-11-16 confirming Community Edition availability under GPL-3.
licence: GPL-3.0 (Community Edition); Enterprise and Infinigraph editions are commercially licensed
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 on Community Edition: embedding in a distributed product triggers copyleft, which is the deliberate commercial boundary. Enterprise features (clustering, role-based access control, multi-database) require a paid licence at a price not publicly listed.
costs: Community Edition: no licence fee, free download (verified 2026-11-16). Enterprise/Infinigraph: quote required, no public price. AuraDB: Free $0; Professional from $0.09/GB/hour (min 1GB); Business Critical from $0.20/GB/hour (min 2GB); Virtual Dedicated Cloud contact sales — hourly metering includes storage, compute, IO, network and backups (all verified 2026-11-16, USD). Self-hosting infrastructure: a JVM host with substantial RAM. Estimate for self-hosting.
privacy: Self-hosted Community Edition keeps the graph entirely on your infrastructure. AuraDB places it with the vendor, which for an investigation graph containing leak-derived entities is a significant custody decision.
alternatives: DuckDB with recursive SQL for many relationship queries without a graph database
NetworkX or igraph for analysis without persistence
Kùzu — AVOID, archived as of 2025-10-10
blockers: Community Edition lacks access control and clustering; Enterprise pricing is quote-only
